chunks.text: USING THE CFC BEEF FEEDER GROWOUT MODEL The CFC Beef Feeder Growout Model allows you to define and simulate a complete growout model. All predictive equations, multiplier defaults, and adjustment factor defaults are from the NRC Nutrient Requirements of Beef Cattle, Seventh Revised Edition, 1996, with NRC 2000 modifications. The model’s straightforward design and total flexibility allows you to define: the desired energy multipliers and dry matter adjustment factors for their respective predictive equations; the rations to be used and how they will be fed in the model; herd data; monetary data. The growout is then simulated and provides summaries for performance, economics, total ration usage, and the growout detail for every day the animals are on feed. The beef system is linked to the Concept5 formulation system to allow any stored ration within Concept5 to be used in the model. You may maintain several levels or stages of intermediate feeds. When a premix formula is revised, the nutrient profile and cost of the equivalent ingredient is automatically updated. As a result, subsequent formulation of higher level feeds using the premix properly reflects premix revisions. This automatic, multi-level link between feeds is also important when projecting ingredient requirements based on finished feed tonnage forecasts. A correct computation of raw ingredient requirements must include the raw material components of each intermediate feed. Traditional least cost formulation software assumes a 100 percent yield of finished product per ton of ingredients mixed. The nutrient composition and cost of the finished product is therefore the same as the nutrient composition and cost of the “as mixed” formula. The formulation of products, which may undergo a significant change in moisture (usually loss) during the manufacturing process, creates several complex issues and challenges for formulators. Nutritional requirements must be met at the Finished Product moisture level, and the cost of the formula per ton of Finished Product must be determined. A means of controlling ingredient inclusion rates must be set up if the inclusion rate must be specified as a function of the finished product weight. Premixes and coatings are good examples of ingredients which should be controlled in this fashion. The formula which minimizes the cost per unit of Finished Product must be determined. This is NOT necessarily the formula which minimizes the cost per ton of the “Raw Mix”.

When the Formulate button is clicked, the ratio results will appear in the solution amount column (Sol Amt). If the ratio is limiting, i.e., it is hitting either the maximum or minimum limit of the ratio, a blue number will be showing in the Minimum or Maximum columns, and a restriction cost will appear in the Rest Cost column. The restriction cost is a per ton cost that applies to a change of one unit (1.0) of the limiting nutrient (numerator) in the ratio. A red number in the either the Minimum or Maximum column means that the ratio cannot be met and the formula is infeasible.
